title: 139 Evaluating effectiveness of several cattle anthelmintics via two fecal egg count reduction tests on ranch raised and auction market calves
content:
Abstract
Parasites negatively impact cattle growth and performance especially on grazing herds. The objective of this study was to compare the efficacy of Valcor (a combination of doramectin/ levamisole) vs doramectin alone, levamisole alone, and negative control using a fecal egg count reduction (FECR) test and growth performance in beef steers. Two studies were performed in 2024 at the University of Arkansas Beef Cattle Research Unit located in Savoy, Arkansas. For study one conducted in July, steer calves from the Savoy cow herd (n = 80; BW = 276 kg) were assigned to one of four treatment groups after being fecal sampled at d -7. Calves were ranked by their d -7 fecal egg count (FEC) and then grouped into four blocks containing 20 animals per block. Within each block, calves were assigned randomly to one of four treatment groups. Treatment groups were: 1) Negative control; 2) doramectin injectable; 3) levamisole drench; 4) doramectin + levamisole injectable (Valcor). FEC and bodyweights were collected on days -7, 0, 14, 28, and 42. Calves were grazed together and maintained on grass pastures for the duration of the study. FEC and growth performance data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS 9.4. Significance was declared at P < 0.05 and tendencies were observed between 0.05 ≤ P < 0.10. The results indicated that mean FEC was decreased (P < 0.0001) with every treatment method when compared to the negative control. On days 14 and 28 post-treatment, doramectin had a 66% and 42% FECR, levamisole had a 99% and 61% FECR, and Valcor had a 99% and 89% FECR, respectively. There were no significant differences in average daily gain (ADG) between the treatment groups. For study two conducted in October, calves purchased at livestock auctions in Arkansas and Oklahoma (n = 91; BW = 222 kg) were separated into bulls and steers and then allocated to one of four treatment groups based on their d -3 FEC. FEC and bodyweights were collected on days -3, 0, 14, 28, and 42. Data were analyzed by the MIXED procedure of SAS 9.4. All calves receiving a dewormer had lower (P < 0.0001) FEC than the negative control. On days 14 and 28 post-treatment, doramectin had an 83% and 79% FECR, levamisole had a 99% and 98% FECR, and Valcor had a 99% and 99% FECR, respectively. Through 28 days post-treatment, ADG was greater (P = 0.048) for calves treated with Valcor and levamisole compared to calves treated with doramectin or the negative control. ADG was 0.75, 0.71, 0.45, and 0.52 kg for each group, respectively. These data suggest that treating cattle with Valcor suppresses parasite population the longest and can improve cattle performance.
